title: The NDIS Roster Looks Full. The Travel Between Visits Is Where the Margin Goes.
excerpt: World Mental Health Day puts community mental health work in the spotlight, but for NDIS providers a fully rostered day can still bleed margin in the travel time between visits that never reaches an invoice.
content:
Ten October is World Mental Health Day, and most of the week's attention rightly goes to psychologists, counsellors and GPs. Less visible is the community support work sitting underneath a lot of that care: the home visits, outreach sessions and psychosocial recovery supports delivered by NDIS providers across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, usually one participant and one suburb at a time.

For these providers, the roster is the business. A full week of scheduled visits looks like a strong week, and in most service businesses it would be. In disability support delivery, a full roster and a profitable one are not automatically the same thing, and the gap between them sits in a place most monthly reporting never actually looks: the time spent driving between one visit and the next.

That time is a real cost. It is wages, vehicle expense and a slice of the working day that could otherwise go toward a billable support. Whether it is also lost revenue depends entirely on how the roster was built, and for most owner-led providers, nobody has ever actually costed it that way.

The Hour That Never Makes It Onto an Invoice

The NDIS Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits allow providers to claim a portion of travel time and vehicle cost against some support items, but the claimable amount is capped and rarely stretches to cover the true cost of moving a support worker from one participant's home to the next. For outreach and community-based psychosocial supports in particular, where visits tend to be shorter and more frequent than a block of personal care, travel can make up a meaningful share of a worker's rostered day without making up any share of what actually gets billed.

A support worker rostered for six hours in the field might deliver four and a half billable hours and spend the rest moving between addresses. On the roster, that worker had a full day. In the profit and loss, a day and a half of wage cost each week never touched a claimable support item at all. Multiply that across a team of ten or fifteen workers and the gap stops being a rounding error and starts being the difference between a service line that pays for itself and one that quietly doesn't.

Why a Full Day on the Roster Isn't the Same as a Profitable One

The providers who feel this hardest are usually the ones covering the widest geographic spread, outer Brisbane, regional Queensland, or the outer suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne, where participant density is lower and the distance between visits stretches out accordingly. A roster built purely around participant availability, rather than participant location, can show the same hours delivered as one built with geography in mind, while producing a noticeably different margin at the end of the month.

The comparison that makes this visible is support coordination against direct outreach delivery. Support coordination is typically billed in blocks of office or phone-based time with comparatively little travel attached. Community-based psychosocial and outreach supports carry a very different cost shape, more visits, shorter each time, more distance between them. A provider delivering both under one ABN is effectively running two businesses with two different margin profiles, and a single blended view of revenue against wage cost hides which one is actually carrying the other.

There is a workforce cost sitting alongside the financial one. Support workers who spend large parts of the day driving rather than supporting tend to feel it in job satisfaction well before anyone sees it in the numbers, and turnover in disability support work is expensive to absorb. Recruitment, screening checks and the months it takes a new worker to build trust with participants all compound the cost of a roster that was never built with travel in mind.

Reading the Roster Like a Margin Report, Not Just a Schedule

Most rostering software tracks hours worked and hours billed. Very few providers overlay that against the geography of where each visit actually happens, or against the mix of support types being delivered, which is usually the clearest way to see where the margin in a support delivery business is really sitting. A workforce capacity and utilisation review does exactly that, mapping billable, travel and administrative time against the roster to show which regions, which support types and which rostering patterns are quietly carrying the business, and which ones are being delivered at a cost nobody has added up.

None of this is a comment on the quality or the need for the support being delivered, which rightly sits with the people doing the work. It is a comment on the numbers sitting underneath the roster, and those are worth a second look from time to time. For a provider whose participant base has grown without anyone revisiting how the roster is actually built, a fractional CFO brings exactly that outside view, and a discovery call is a reasonable place to start.

faqs.q: Why can a fully rostered NDIS support day still lose money for the provider?
faqs.a: A roster measures hours scheduled, not hours billed. Travel between participant visits is real wage and vehicle cost but is only partly claimable under the price guide, so a day that looks completely full can still have a sizeable chunk of unpaid, non-billable time sitting inside it.

faqs.q: How much travel time can an NDIS provider actually claim under the price guide?
faqs.a: The NDIS Pricing Arrangements allow a capped claim for provider travel against certain support items, but the allowance is modest and rarely covers the full wage and vehicle cost of moving between visits, particularly for shorter, more frequent community-based supports.

faqs.q: What is a realistic billable utilisation rate for disability support workers?
faqs.a: It varies by support type and geography, which is exactly why a single target figure is unreliable. A workforce capacity and utilisation review maps billable, travel and administrative time against each worker's actual roster rather than relying on an industry rule of thumb.

faqs.q: Does rostering participant visits by suburb actually improve provider margin?
faqs.a: Clustering visits by location reduces the travel time sitting inside each worker's day, which directly lifts the proportion of rostered hours that are actually billable. The effect is usually largest for providers covering outer-metropolitan or regional areas, where distances between participants are greatest.

faqs.q: Why is staff turnover so costly for disability support providers in Queensland?
faqs.a: Recruitment, screening checks and the months it takes a new worker to build trust with participants all represent cost without matching revenue. A roster that burns workers out through heavy, unplanned travel adds to that turnover, compounding a cost that rarely shows up on a single month's P&L.

faqs.q: How can an NDIS provider see where its margin is actually leaking?
faqs.a: Most providers can see total revenue and total wage cost without being able to see which support types, regions or rostering patterns are actually profitable. A fractional CFO brings the structure to separate the two and show exactly where attention will move the margin.
